newsitem.title: HAITI: General strike shuts down Haiti.
newsitem.headline: General strike shuts down Haiti.

text.p: Most businesses and schools were closed on Thursday by a general strike called by popular organisations that oppose Haiti's economic recovery plan.

Sporadic rock-throwing incidents were reported in the capital and United Nations workers were airlifted from Cap-Haitien because of unrest there, but heightened police patrols appeared to maintain relative calm early in the day, officials said.

"Everything is pretty quiet in Port-au-Prince today," U.N. spokeswoman Patricia Tome said on Thursday morning, despite threats of violence as the strike began on Wednesday against anyone who ventured into the streets.

Burning tires and barricades, usually set up by protesters to show discontent, were not yet seen, either due to the rain or the increased police presence in the streets. But a small group of protesters threw rocks and smashed the windscreens of cars driving through the Port-au-Prince suburb of Delmas.
"It was a gamble to go out," one of the few taxi drivers working said. "I need money, but a new windscreen is expensive, too."

The popular organisations that called the strike were demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Rosny Smarth and a change in the country's economic plan, in which nine state-run enterprises will be privatised.

In the northern city of Cap-Haitien, where the strike began on Wednesday, barricades were still in place. At least three people were wounded in a clash between police and protesters on Wednesday, but the mood was more relaxed on Thursday, according to U.N. sources.
The office of the U.N. Civilian Mission was closed and 10 workers were flown out of the city by helicopter.
President Rene Preval has continued to support Smarth, and Smarth has said he will not resign unless asked to by Preval.

Preval acknowledged the dissatisfaction of those who called the strike, but said he did not plan to give in to the organisations' demands. "A relatively small group of people cannot bring the country to a halt unless the population agrees with them," he said after a Wednesday protest.

A representative of one of hundreds of popular organisations said to be sponsoring the strike threatened in a radio address on Wednesday that if the streets were not empty they would "run with red, red red."

An umbrella group calling itself "Koupe Tet, Boule Kay," the Creole words for "Cutting Heads and Burning Houses" after the rallying cry of Haiti's bloody 1803 slave revolt, sent facsimile messages to businesses in Port-au-Prince warning them to close their doors.
Port-au-Prince has been rocked by gang violence in recent days. At least 19 people have been killed, including three police officers, according to the United Nations.
Last week the Justice Ministry's security chief was shot to death and a senator was shot in the head but survived.
The general strike was the second in two months. During the first, on Jan. 16, protesters burned tires and threw rocks in the streets and most residents stayed home.

Foreign soldiers have helped maintain security in Haiti since a U.S.-led military force landed in September 1994 and restored Haiti's then-President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. U.N. peacekeepers, now numbering about 1,500, were scheduled to leave on July 31.
